utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Mr. Jovan Vujinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. I do understand no applications for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vujinovic. I'm speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, before you give evidence in this court you are required to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to stand and make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujinovic. Please be seated. Mr. Vujinovic, you will be first examined by Ms. Gustafson. Ms. Gustafson is sitting to your right. There she is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. Could you please state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Jovan Vujinovic, my father's name, late Jovan from Oton.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided with hard copies of his statements in B/C/S and if he could be shown 65 ter 4920, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I've read it already. It doesn't really matter. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, on the screen in front of you and in the first hard copy statement you have there, do you recognise this as a statement you made and signed on the 20th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, on page 2 of that statement, in the middle of page 2, you described how you were taken by soldiers to a building near the Oton railway stop on the morning of the 18th of August, 1995, and I'd like to read a passage from your statement to you and give you an opportunity to correct it. In your statement you said, "When these soldiers were leaving they took me with them. The soldiers took me to their HQ, i.e., field HQ. The HQ was in a building at a railway stop known as railway stop Oton. There, I saw a number of officers, a telex machine, a mobile phone in one person's hand and many other soldiers. I also saw a number of military vehicles bearing HV number plates." I'd like to ask you, did you consider this building to be the soldier's HQ or the field HQ at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You explained in your statement that you were taken to an HQ at a building near the railway stop in Oton. Is that correct? Did you consider that to be the HQ at the time or did you consider it to be something else?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: It was not an HQ. It was when all the villagers escaped, it was clearing up really, they were collecting cattle from houses. So it wasn't really any kind of centre for soldiers, but they used it as accommodations to sleep over at night, so it wasn't really any sort of command. I just referred to it as a command but it wasn't really a command.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And with that correction, do you consider this statement that you made in 1999 to be true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I've just said now, that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And with that correction, is the statement that you made in 1999, the one that's on the screen in front of you, is it true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes, that's how it was. This was -- I won't say looting, but they were just clearing up the villages. Everything was deserted. The Serbs and the paramilitary, everything was cleansed and they just took stuff, what -- that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If I could ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, I think it would be easier if you look to Ms. Gustafson who is standing over there because she's putting the questions to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know. I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it facilitates your communication. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And does this statement that you made in 1999 that's on the screen, does it accurately reflect what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. That's how it was. Briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if I asked you in court today the same questions that you were asked when you made that statement, would you give the Court the same answers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe I would have some corrections. I don't know. It depends. This is it, but it depends on what you're going to ask me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, did you read this statement over in the last couple of days, a few days ago?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And apart from the correction that we just went over, if I asked you the same questions today in court, would you give the same answers that are in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I certainly would. Except for the error, what I said before, that it was a command. It wasn't really a command nor was this active troops. This was just clearing up of houses and looting, but there was no killing or -- nor was this an army. It was just clearing up, taking cattle away. Looting, let's call it that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown 65 ter number 4921, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, do you recognise this statement as one that you made and signed on the 12th of October, 2004?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot really see this without my glasses, but go ahead, put the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you have your glasses with you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Just ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether this is the statement you gave and whether you recognise it. So you can't answer that question apparently without your glasses. Do you have glasses with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already read all of this before and everything was correct there. You didn't add anything to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But my last question was whether you have your glasses with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't. There is nothing to read. I've read this already, yesterday and the day before yesterday and even before when they came to my house to Croatia, I also read it then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least you think it's the same, isn't it, and most likely it will be the same but we would like you to look at that. Could you tell us where your glasses are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No glasses here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is no need, but okay, if you insist, I'll read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could read and recognise the hard copy that he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why don't you read and I will answer your question. If you have it, just read it. You read it out to me and then I will reply whether it's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic -- Mr. Vujinovic, what we are trying to do is to avoid that we have to go through all of this again. So if you look at the statement and if you recognise it as yours, then we can move on more quickly. Could you -- we are now talking about the -- this statement now, the second one was --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 4921.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Dated the 12th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 12th of October. Mr. Usher, have you verified that the 12th of October statement is in the hands of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, yeah, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's your statement, Mr. Vujinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, whose would it be? There is no one else but me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please -- okay, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to make one correction which I think for purposes of accuracy of the record, his name is misspelled on the statement. So it should be with that correction, that's what the statement is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's true, this is the issue of the name. I understood that the witness doesn't bear the same name as most of his family members due to a mistake in registration when he was born. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe this morning he actually said Vujinovic was his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then verify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is corrected explicitly in the third statement so if it's tendered into evidence, I believe that would serve --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps with the third statement, you specifically ask for this point. Yes. So the second one, Mr. Vujinovic, same questions. If these matters would be raised again, if questions would be put to you, would you give the same answers as -- I don't know whether there's any correction to be made, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a similar reference to the HQ but I consider that to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be covered. Is that understood? Yes. I see Defence counsel understand the previous correction as well. If we would put the same questions as you answered in that statement, would you give the same answers, Mr. Vujinovic? We are now talking about the second statement. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as my name is concerned, it's not really my name, it's my last name. There is just an "I" missing. In some places it says Vujnovic and in others it says Vujinovic. And the registration was -- said Vujinovic. On the other hand, everyone, all my family members are Vujnovic without the "I" and lately we've tried to correct it. But as far as that is concerned, there is no problem. It's the same name, there is just an error that was made at registration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I come back to my question. You've just been shown a document of which you said who else his statement could it be. If the same questions would be put to you, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson, with the third and final.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 65 ter number 4922 is the third statement and if the usher could provide the witness with his 2007 statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you recognise that, Mr. Vujinovic, as a statement that you made and signed on the 4th of April, 2007?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever it says in there, it's correct. If you have additional questions, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like to make sure that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, excuse me. It's just previously, Mr. President, when you asked the question, there was no interpretation of his answer. When you asked whether or not if you were asked the same questions again you would -- it just says no interpretation, it doesn't say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I heard the witness clearly say "da" which means yes for me but I haven't checked whether it's on the transcript. If everyone has heard the same, then I take it that we can agree that he said "da." Yes. Please proceed. Thank you, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, I would just like you to recognise -- to look at that statement and make sure that you recognise it as yours. Do you recognise it? Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And is it and true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, it should be because how could I tell you about anything unless -- except on the basis of what I saw? I remained all alone in the village, no one touched me. And on the 24th of 9th, I was in Knin. My house was set on fire and there were fires everywhere. It's not really the fault of the Croatian army, they did not kill, but there were fools on all sides. There were idiots on all sides and my mother was killed also on the 17th, but it's not the Croatian army. These were the people who looted, these idiots. They told me, you know, you should go away, there are idiots everywhere but I didn't want to leave. And no one ever touched me. On the 24th of September, I continued working until the 1st of August, 1995, I worked for the railway and then on the 24th September also in 1995, I came to the office to look for some papers and -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to focus as much as you can on the precise question that I ask you and answer just that question.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This 2007 statement that you have in front of you, if I asked you the same questions that you were asked when you gave that statement, would you give the Court the same answers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to tender those three statements into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 04920 becomes Exhibit number P412.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the 1999 statement. P412 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 04921, that's the 2004 statement, becomes Exhibit P413.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P413 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And 65 ter number 04922, that's the 2007 statement, becomes Exhibit number P414.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P414 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, the Court has your statements and they now have all the information that's in your statements. So I'm just going to ask you a few details about things that aren't in your statements and I'd like to ask you again to focus as much as you can on the specific question that I ask and direct your answer to that specific question.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You explained in your statement that about 200 people lived in Oton Polje before Operation Storm. What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: They were all Serbs. There were no Croats. But during the war, no one was wounded or killed in my village, no one was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vujinovic, try to focus precisely on the question. The question was not whether people were killed but just what the ethnicity of the inhabitants was. So try to -- and if Ms. Gustafson wants to know more, she'll certainly ask you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: How far was your house from the building next to the Oton railway station where the soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: About 356 metres and I know because I measured the hose because I took water from a water fountain there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you one or two questions about Stevo Vujnovic from Oton Polje whose death you talk about in your statements. And I'd just like to start with some personal details about Stevo Vujnovic. Was he born in Oton or was he born elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: In Oton.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what was his father's name?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Ivan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did he have a brother who lived in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Zagreb, but I'm not sure where they lived. They are all dead, only the brother Momcilo is alive. Everyone else is dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: What was the name of the brother who lived in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: His name was Djuro, also Vujnovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in August 1995, was Stevo Vujnovic a soldier or was he a civilian?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: He was a civilian. He wasn't in any army.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you've explained at paragraph 3 of your 2004 statement how you found Stevo Vujnovic's body in the yard of his house and that seven or eight days later, you took some policemen that were in the area to the place -- to his house where his body was still lying in the same spot. On that day, when you showed the policemen the location of Stevo Vujnovic's body, did those policemen ask you any questions about how Stevo Vujnovic had died?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't ask me that question because that's 1.5 to 2 kilometres away from my house, so nothing was said about how he was killed. I heard that later. I went to see. I saw him dead in front of the house. I reported that to the police. And then after that, that organisation, the Red Cross or something, they took him and wrapped him up and took him away. I mean that's the whole philosophy of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in your 2007 statement at paragraph 5, you explained how everyone in your hamlet except for yourself and two people who were infirm left Oton Polje on the 21st of August, 1995, with the assistance of a Ukrainian monitor named Pero and I'd like to ask you if you had any conversations with Pero when he came to your hamlet?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Pero Ukrajnici [phoen] is not correct. I spoke with him, he came to see me a couple of times, drank wine and Schnapps. I said to him, Pero, you drink like a Russian, do you know that expression? Because when they left on the 5th, the last group left on the 5th and then it was the 21st of May and he was touring the villages and then after that, he went to the barracks in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In your answer, you just said the 21st of May. Is that -- do you mean the 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: The 21st of August. Yes, yes, it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to you to think back to the conversations you had with Pero. Did you tell Pero what had happened to your mother?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was there. He came to visit me a couple of times. They lived in Knin and then they would come to the villages and they would drop by to my place for a drink, the soldiers were also dropping by. They would eat and drink. Nobody touched me. Nobody did anything to me but then on that day when there was looting and things, there was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you ever report what had happened to your mother to the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: There was nothing to report. The people were going around. What could I do? I reported it only when I read in something -- I still have that at home, when they were asking for reparation, then I contacted a lawyer in Split and she drafted that request for reparation. And then when it was time when the case came up, they just declared that my mother was killed. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did anyone from the Croatian police or the Croatian military ever take a statement from you or ask you any questions about what had happened to your mother?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't -- nobody asked me any questions. Well, yes, actually the police came and the people from The Hague, they came, they took photographs, and they told me not to touch anything around the place where she was killed. And it's still the same there behind the house some 80 metres away. It's not disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said the police came and the people from The Hague, they came. And I'd like you to clarify that answer. Investigators from The Hague came and spoke with you. Did anyone from the Croatian police come and speak to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't report it to the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is there a hamlet called Oton Brdo near Oton Polje?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's also a village. It's a hamlet, Brdo, Bender and Oton Polje. There is Oton Polje, Oton Brdo and Oton Bender. It's all just one village and these are its hamlets. That's the -- what their names are.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And Oton Brdo and Oton Bender, are those also Serb hamlets?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Oton Brdo was a hamlet of two or three Croat houses. There were two or three Croat houses there, but they also left with the Serb refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And approximately how many people lived in Oton Brdo before Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't say that. Brdo Oton and Bender are smaller hamlets than Oton Brdo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Polje, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And how many people stayed behind in Oton Brdo after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I was there with the commission from the Knin municipality when they were taking down the numbers. In Plavno, there was 131; Oton Bender, there were 14 left; Oton Brdo, 33. Oton Polje where I was, there was just me and a grandmother. She was sick and this international community was giving her food. In Padjine, there was 16. In this village, there was 26. In Raducici, 27. I went when they were taking down these numbers with a lawyer from the Knin municipality and there was also two lawyers from Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And, again, could you try and focus as much as you can on the specific question that I ask you. Do you know two individuals named Branko Sudar and Ilija Sudar from Oton Brdo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we know each other. I don't know when they were killed though.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did they stay behind after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I think that they did. Actually, I don't know if they did or didn't. I don't know. All I know is that they were killed. I didn't see it but I heard it and I knew this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When did you hear that? Approximately?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I heard it later, a month later, 15 days later. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When would that have been? You say a month later, 15 days later, what month and year was it when you heard about their deaths?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe -- well, it was after Storm but I have no idea when. All I heard was that they were killed and then I established that they actually were.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to their bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: One of them was buried at the cemetery. As for the other one, I have no idea. I don't know -- well this is in the neighbouring villages, Brdo and Bender but I don't know exactly about that, but all I do know is they were killed; or, rather, I heard this. I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you know how old they were at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Pasic and Sudar, Branko, Branko was 36 years old but I don't know about the other one. I think the other one was younger. Sudar, Ilija or whatever his name was, Ilija, he was older.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you know a woman named Djuka Zunic from Oton Brdo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know her, she was an elderly woman. I don't know if somebody threw her into a well or if she drowned herself. I don't know. Nobody ever determined what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said, "I don't know if somebody threw her into a well or if she drowned herself." Was her body found in a well?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. So that's how they saw that she drowned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And approximately when was this?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you. Well, it was during that period. I don't know that myself. I just heard it. I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said "during that period," could you be more specific, a month and a year?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: 1995. As for the month, I don't know if it was August or September. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you know a man named Nikola Pasic from Oton Bender?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a blacksmith. I knew him, he worked for the railways. That's all I know about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you hear of anything happening to him after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that he was killed. I didn't see it myself, but I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And was this also something you heard in -- around August or September?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vujinovic. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Usually, a summary is read. I don't know whether you for any specific purpose refrained from doing it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, it was just an omission. I could read it now if that would suit the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, because the public doesn't know what is in your statement, apart from what you told us in addition to these statements, Ms. Gustafson will now read a summary. You don't have to respond. It's not questions, it's just that everyone knows what was in your statement. Just listen carefully. After she's read it, you will be examined by counsel for the Defence. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you for the reminder. Jovan Vujinovic lived in the hamlet of Oton Polje in Ervenik municipality at the time of Operation Storm. Prior to Operation Storm, approximately 200 people lived in 60 households in this hamlet. Most of those people left the hamlet between 4th and 5th of August, 1995, including everyone in the witness's family except himself and his elderly mother. Most of the approximately 17 persons who remained were elderly. On 5th August, 1995, Croatian soldiers entered the hamlet and began looting. The looting continued for several weeks. On 18 August 1995, the witness was away from his house for several hours. When he returned home, his house had been destroyed by fire and he discovered his dead mother approximately 80 metres from his house with three bullet holes in her face. Eleven houses in the hamlet were destroyed by fire that day. On 21 or 22nd August, 1995, the witness found the dead body of another villager, Stevo Vujnovic lying dead in front of his house in a pool of blood. Seven or eight days later, his body was still there and the witness took some policemen who were in the area to the location of the body. The policemen did not take the body away that day. On the 21st of August, 1995, all remaining persons in Oton Polje except for the witness and two others, both of whom were infirm, left Oton Polje with the assistance of international monitors. The witness heard that they were taken to the UN barracks in Knin and later transported to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Mr. Misetic, and I'm also addressing other counsel, as far as the level of abstract thinking versus facts is concerned, I expect from all of you to stay on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Will do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vujinovic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to start by asking you some questions about the first day of Operation Storm which is 4 August 1995. You mention it in your statement and you said that your family left around 1300 hours on the 4th. Do you recall that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You also say in your statement that they left because there were RSK officials, some wearing military uniform that told the people to leave because the Ustasha forces were coming. Do you recall that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement that these RSK officials that were wearing military uniform began to distribute fuel for the purposes of leaving. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. What do I know? That organisation that was there was distributing this to uniforms and civilians. I don't know exactly how it was. In any case, they were distributing it and there were threats that they needed to leave. Actually nobody was driving them out, they all left voluntarily, all of them. Nobody was driving anyone away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: When you say "they left voluntarily" who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: All the civilians who left. In my opinion, they all left voluntarily. I was among them. Nobody was driving me away or telling me to go. I guess they were just listening to those organisations that were there, the Chetnik ones and what do I know? That's why they left. Nobody was driving anyone out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These RSK officials, some of whom were wearing military uniform, did you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: We all know each other or knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: These officials, were they people from your local area?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your village was not shelled on the 4th of August, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. Nobody was killed in the war and nobody was wounded. There was no war there. There were no -- there was no combat in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Going forward now, talking about the village by Ukrainian Pero, you say in your statement that Ukrainian Pero encouraged the remaining villagers to leave but you decided you were going to stay and in your 2007 statement at page 5, you say you felt safe because Croatian police you knew -- because Croatian police whom you knew from before Operation Storm --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I just -- the reference to Ukrainian Pero encouraged remaining villagers to leave. I'm not sure where that is in the witness' statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I take it that you are able to help Ms. Gustafson out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I read about the assistance but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, just one moment, Your Honour. It's actually in his supplemental information sheet, Your Honour. What we received from the Prosecution says: "Pero asked the witness to leave the village with the other villagers who left but the witness didn't want to."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you consider to be the supplemental information sheet. Have we received a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't think it's in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we should -- then it's -- of course you can ask questions about, no problem, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Then it's leading but it's leading on the basis of what the Prosecution gave me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leading, as such, in cross-examination appears not to be a very bad thing to do. The only thing is that if you refer to a statement, the Chamber of course will try to find in the statement and finds no basis for your questions, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, it's actually in his supplemental sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your discussions with the Office of the Prosecutor in the past few days, you told the Prosecutor that Pero asked you to leave the village with the other villagers but that you decided to stay. And in your 2007 --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in your 2007 statement, at page 5 -- sorry, at paragraph 5, you say, "I did not fear remaining in the village. Croatian police who I knew from before Operation Storm would often drink at my house and so I felt safe." Is that accurate that you felt safe because of the presence of these Croatian policemen?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian army would come to my place every day, they would come to drink. The police did stop by as well. Nobody touched me. After Storm, they looked for me. They gave me an apartment. Then I retired. Nobody touched me. The soldiers, the police would sit at my place, the international community people also did. They would come to my place as if it was the military command. I was by myself. I was the only one left in the village. We would sit there, we would chat, we would drink.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I'd like to call up -- this is basically to admit this into evidence. It is a 65 ter exhibit of the Prosecution. 65 ter 4132, it's an incident report by CIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to tender that from the bar table as relevant in the context of the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I actually am going to ask him to comment on it a bit. It was on the -- I thought the Prosecution was going to admit it but if they won't, I'll tender it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I believe it's already Exhibit P234, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could we have P234 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, do you recall if Pero's name was really Petro or did you just call him Pero?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: He introduced himself to me as Pero Ukrajinac [phoen]. He spoke six foreign languages and said that he had been in the foreign legion. He spoke Croatian perfectly so everyone understood him. But anyway, he told me that he spoke six foreign languages but he spoke Croatian just as I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Pero wrote a report on the 24th of August. The person I'm assuming to be Pero. And in the report, he says that according to his information, Stevo Vujnovic was found by people from the village dead along with his mother Marija Vujnovic in their house approximately on 12/8/95. Do you recall if maybe these people were found on the 12th and not seven or eight days after your mother was killed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: They were found -- well, actually, an old lady was passing by there and she saw Stevo Vujnovic dead. Later when I went to check, I also saw him. He was lying on his stomach. His mother, she was sick, she was lying in bed. Nobody went inside that house. Nobody went there. Nobody looked after her. And even though we sort of looked out for her, there was a stink so nobody went into the house. And when her son Momcilo came back from Serbia, he said he went into the house and found her in bed and that she was dead. But nobody went in so I really couldn't say if this was like that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, Mr. Registrar, I'd like to call up and tender into evidence the autopsy report for Stevo Vujnovic, 1D29-0009. I'm sorry, it could be 1D29-0003. I apologise. Your Honour, one moment just to make sure we have the right ... Can we turn to the next page? And to the next page? There it is. Your Honour, I will tender it from the bar table. I have to get the ID number to match with the decedent.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's our opinion that this is the autopsy report of Stevo Vujnovic and there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. If could go back to page 1, please. Under cause of death, the cause of death is unascertained. Your Honour, I would ask that this exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence as the autopsy report for Stevo Vujnovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D383.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D383 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D29-0027.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, I'm going to show you a map of the locality where you are from. You were -- you used to work on the railway so I assume you're familiar somewhat with maps from the area and if I'm wrong, please correct me. Is my assumption correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we turn to page 2 of this exhibit. And the B/C/S version of this, Mr. Registrar, is 1D29-0024, just so the witness can see the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Witness, you can see -- let me -- do you see Knin on the bottom right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I see Oton.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then that line goes straight down to Knin, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, Oton is up in the upper left-hand corner; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the middle of the page is what I have marked in a red circle Padjine, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that where, prior to Operation Storm, there was a military barracks of the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure whether the witness said yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: So in Padjene and in Stara Straza. There was in Padjene and in Stara Straza there were barracks, military barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And those were the two red circles, the one on the right being the Stara Straza barracks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, if you say yes, is it because you read it, Stara Straza or is it because you recognise on the map the location exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm looking at it and I can see it. And I know it, I also know it personally and I can also tell from the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we can go to the next page, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now a close-up of your hamlet.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Oton Polje or Oton field. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if you see on the right towards the middle, there is a circle which I have marked as the railway stop that you refer to in your statement. Is that the location of the railway stop; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the railway stop. It's still a railway stop today as before. That's exactly where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And to the left of that, where there is a big circle, is that the general area of where your property is located in Oton?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: To the left where my name is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Is that what you mean? Yes. Yes, it's right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I ask would ask that this be marked and I tender this into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D384, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D384 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The -- during Operation Storm itself, did you see any Serb soldiers taking up any positions at the location known as Debelo Brdo on about the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your 1999 statement, Witness, you say: "Between the 5th of August, 1995, and 18 August 1995, there were no tragic incidents in our hamlet, just looting." No houses in your hamlet were set on fire --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- no houses were set on fire between 5 August and 18 August in your hamlet, were they?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Approximately those dates, but maybe it was before as well. I think there were 13 or 17 in total. I'm not exactly sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in one of your statements, you say that there were 60 households in your hamlet. Would 60 households mean there were 60 houses? Do you know actually how many actual houses there were in the hamlet?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: About 50. 50, 60, I'm not sure. Up to 50 households.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you found your mother, you buried her immediately; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I found her on the 17th at night. She was dead, and we buried her on the 21st of August. She had already begun to smell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You did not report to these Croatian -- you reported the death of -- you said on questions by Ms. Gustafson, you reported the death of Stevo Vujnovic to the police but you didn't report the death of your mother to the police; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. We didn't even know that my mother was dead. We just reported his death, Stevo. We did not report my mother's death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Because we didn't see it. We didn't enter. There was no one who could enter and see.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I wonder if that last answer could be clarified. I think there might be confusion as to whose mother ... THE COURT: Last three answers, preferably. Not reporting -- the witness is not aware of his mother having died is, of course, leaves -- he is certainly became aware at a certain moment, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: After you buried your mother, you still did not report your mother's death to the Croatian police officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't really remember because we reported to the police, they were writing down the houses that had been set on fire, and how would you report it? I mean there was no one to report it to. This was the Zadar-Knin municipality district. They only came to Knin up to 1400 hours. After 1400 hours, they went back. So there was no one to report to. I only reported when I asked for compensation or reparations and that's when I reported her and that's when she was proclaimed dead. Up until that moment, she was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Registrar, to follow on this answer, if we could have 1D29-0018.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, Witness, being present for an on-site investigation by the Croatian police at the grave site of your mother on or about the 17th of April, 2007?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the police came on several occasions and they said they couldn't do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall an investigator of the Croatian police named Robert Badzim [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall giving information to an investigator of the Croatian police concerning the death of your mother in 2007?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: They came on several occasions. I don't recall exactly the date when this happened, but they came and people asked me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's nothing that I can comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd ask that the exhibit on the screen be marked and I tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D385, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D385 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Vujinovic, could I ask you, you said the police came at several occasions. Could you tell us when, for the first time, they came, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember. I can't recall now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it all last year or was it in any ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in the same year. Everyone knew that she had been killed. The police knew. The military knew. So they came to write it down. I don't know if this was an active soldier or not. They all wore uniforms. The police knew about it. The military knew about it. How would you tell? How could you tell? I mean this was organised then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that you said they came for the first time during the summer that it had happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what he testified, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic. I read the transcript. It was in the same year, everyone knew, the police knew, so I'm seeking clarification of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that we -- that the witness doesn't get confused. I believe earlier he testified that they started to come after he filed a claim for compensation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. I nevertheless prefer to be able to put my questions. You said "Everyone knew, knew that she had been killed." What are you talking about? Are you talking about last year? Are you talking about the summer when it happened? Any years in between when they came for the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened the same year, the same month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same month of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It didn't -- this wasn't just about me. In 1995, the military and the police, they kept coming to my place. They knew that she was killed. She was killed like an animal and that's what they were commenting on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you told them about it and it was part of your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They knew about it but they can't be -- it couldn't be their fault, I mean, if some idiot killed her. Maybe, maybe someone, the Chetniks killed some of their family members so it was really hard to tell. Nobody knew who killed her or why she was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it was part of your conversation when the military and the police came to your place, is that in the summer when it happened? Is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, every day, the police and the military came to my place. There was barely a day when they didn't come, so this was like that from 1995 onwards. And different organisations came and aid from Switzerland, whenever anything like that came, they would come to me. So then I had to go and see the neighbours and show them where someone had remained or so -- there was also from Holland and from Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, what I'm interested in at this moment and I want you to listen very carefully to my question. In the summer that your mother died, did you already, in that summer when, as you told us, the police came to your house, did you already discuss and talk about the death of your mother with the police that came to see you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I was following the translation of the witness' answers and I believe in page 29 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no problem if you point at a line where you think there is a mistake of a translation. I, however, would not like you to tell us what the witness said because that could be, I'm not saying that it is, but it could be very suggestive and translations can always be verified on the basis of the original material. So if you say that there is any problem, please point at the line and the -- the page and the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I was not intending to say what the witness said, Your Honour. I was just pointing the line and it was a -- page 29 and line 7. The answer of the witness to the question of Mr. Misetic, what was happened when the police came on the site of the death of his mother. So the answer was, upon my best recollection and knowing the Croatian language, wrongly translated. So maybe the witness could clarify this by another question on the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The witness said, Yes, the police came on several occasions and they said they couldn't do anything about it. That was not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, there is some doubt as to your answer to the following question: "Do you recall, Witness, being present for an on-site investigation by the Croatian police at the grave site of your mother on or about the 17th of April, 2007?" What was your answer to that question? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police came and I suppose on the basis of what they received from The Hague, your officials, they called me from Sibenik and this organisation from The Hague came. I wasn't at home. But they had already come on several occasions earlier. They all came and they said that I shouldn't touch anything where she was buried. They said "Don't touch anything." So I didn't. She lay in her own soil, the Croatian soil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Thank you for -- it's just a matter of procedure, Mr. Mikulicic, that I'm very precise because it often happens that someone then says what the witness is supposed to have said and that's a procedure I'd like to avoid to the extent possible but you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wouldn't do that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on Your Honour's last question, I'd like to pose a question. We will upload the witness' supplemental information sheet into e-court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, Mr. Vujinovic, you spoke to the Office of the Prosecutor a few days ago; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall being asked to read over and sign another correction to your prior witness -- correction and clarification of your earlier witness statements. Do you recall signing another document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: These last couple of days?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall, of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to read back a portion of a document that has your signature on it. It says, "The witness stated that he never reported his mother's death to the Croatian police. At some point, the Croatian authorities came around and made a list of people who stayed in the villages and the witness told them what happened to his mother. Much later, a few years, he also reported his mother's death to the Croatian authorities in Knin." Do you recall telling that to the Prosecutor's office within the last few days?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN VUJINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, when it's loaded into e-court, we will load it into e-court but the witness' supplemental information sheet of 4 June 2008, we would ask for a number and we tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- a portion of that has just been put to the witness and he's agreed to it. I don't see the basis for tendering the entire supplemental into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't see any difference until now because the witness said that he never reported it so that is in his evidence at this moment now, that people came around and made lists is also what he testified today -- whether that is -- and the witness told them what happened to his mother. I understood the testimony of the witness as kind of an informal conversations during that period of time when people came to see him perhaps not in official capacity but apparently frequented his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't see why the additional clarification wouldn't be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from there are no major -- there is no objection to it, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's just that, I mean, the portion that has been put to him has been put to him. There's no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That's then --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- nothing to be added by tendering the entire statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D386.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D386 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, if I could have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, thank you for coming to testify. I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the Cermak Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, any need to put further questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just about to say that, Mr. Vujinovic but you were, as it happened, a couple of times today, you skillfully took over. Mr. Vujinovic, it's right, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions put to you by the parties and put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Am I done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Let me go and light a cigarette. All right. Let's light a cigarette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujinovic, smoking is allowed only outside.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May you stay in good health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that we take an early break. Is the Prosecution ready to call the next witness after the break? Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution calls Mr. Peter Marti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I was informed that the knowledge of the English language by Mr. Marti is good but not perfect. Now, he will not be the only one in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any problem, we'll try to assist the witness in his own language to the extent this would not hurt the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I did discuss this with Mr. Waespi and given the fact that he probably understands best what the witness is trying to convey during the cross -- certainly during the course of our question, I invited Mr. Waespi to please chime in for any clarification he thinks is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Marti. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti. You will give your testimony in the English language. If there's any moment where you have difficulties either in understanding or in expressing yourself in that language, please ask for assistance. I must admit that my Schweitzer-Deutsch is not as it should be, perhaps, but Mr. Waespi is also a native Swiss-German or German-Swiss-speaking person. I understand the language quite well. This is not an invitation to continue in your own language because the interpreters would be lost but if there is any specific matter where you are trying to find a word or something like that and if you are not able to do it, then perhaps say that one word in your own language and then we'll see how we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, can you please state your name, your full name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: My full name is Peter Marti.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you recall giving three statements to the ICTY, one dated 13th February, 1996; one, a taped one on 29th June, 1997, and the third one dated 13th and 14th December, 2007?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission, I would like to provide the witness with copies of these three statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, to be clear, the first statement of February 1996 has the 65 ter number 5176. The transcript of a taped interview originally in German dated 29th June, 1997, has the 65 ter number 5177. And the third one dated 13 and 14 December 2007, has the 65 ter number 5178.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Marti, did you have a chance to review those three statements before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We did it the last days we went through all that documents and we added some small corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me refer you to one of these corrections and this, Your Honours, relates to the taped interview. This is ter number 5177. On page 9, in the English version, lines 32 to 34. In B/C/S, it's on page 9, line 17. I'll read what it says in the English transcript. "So for example on 8 August when we drove through Kistanje, we saw how the town, how the streets were burning and next to it, we saw men in Croatian uniforms standing there ..." and it continues. Mr. Marti, can you let the Court know whether the August 8th is the correct date of that incident or is it a different date in August?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: No, this date is not correct. It was actually the 11th of August when we -- that same day, we came back from Sibenik and we went to patrol. So that was a mistake, it was the 11th, not the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti. There will be more clarifications rather than corrections throughout this morning but with this correction, can you tell the Court whether the information contained in these statements is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do these three statements accurately reflect of what you had said when you were interviewed at those three occasions?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if asked the same questions here in court today, would your answers be the same as recorded in these three statements?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if these three statements could be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first is 65 ter number 05176, this is the statement of 1996. This becomes Exhibit P415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P415 is admitted into evidence because there were no objections as I saw from the submissions, the written submissions by the parties. Mr. Registrar, the second one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The second statement 65 ter number 05177. This is the statement of 1997. And becomes Exhibit number P416.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same is true, as far as I'm aware, for P416 and, therefore, P416 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the third statement, Your Honour, is 65 ter number 5178. This is the statement of 2007 and becomes Exhibit number P417.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since from the written submissions it appears that there are no objections against admission, P417 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I would like to read a brief summary of the witness' evidence as contained in these three statements. Peter Marti was a UN military observer in Team Podkonje within UN Sector South from 19 June 1995 onwards. He became the team leader of Team Podkonje from 6 September to 7 October 1995. From 8 October to 27 November, 1995, he was the Senior Liaison Officer for human rights activities also stationed in Knin. Prior to Operation Storm, Mr. Marti observed shelling around Cetina and conducted crater analyses at a number of occasions. On 4th and 5th August, he observed the shelling of Knin, first from his house in Podkonje and then from the UN headquarters compound. After Operation Storm, Mr. Marti visited many areas throughout Sector South as part of regular UN-UNMO patrols. He witnessed houses and villages burning in the presence of Croatian soldiers. Mr. Marti met with Croatian authorities to discuss issues such as establishing checkpoints. Mr. Marti also became a member of Human Rights Action Teams that reported on incidents of looting, destruction, and killings that occurred subsequent to Operation Storm. Mr. Marti's observations and conclusions are contained in various UNMO reports as well as in his personal diary. This concludes the summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, talking about your diary. Do you have your diary with you today?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I have. It's this diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we have disclosed the original of the diary to the Defence which is in German and the translation of some relevant parts have been -- has been made into English and also disclosed to the Defence but I will not be seeking to tender the diary. But the witness might refer to that source, perhaps with your leave, Mr. President, throughout this examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, whenever you want to rely upon your written notes in your diary, please always indicate that you are doing so. I can't see what is on your desk, both Defence counsel and counsel for the Prosecution usually see what you're doing but I would like to know when you are talking from memory and when you are answering questions on the basis of your diary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, I would like to highlight a few areas that are contained in your statements. First, I'd like to direct your attention to your 2007 statement which is now P417. That's the third statement. In paragraph 24, that's at page 4 in the English version and page 5 in the B/C/S version, you discuss a crater analysis performed by yourself and another UNMO on 9 July 1995 in the village of Vukovici that involved four elderly women. Do you recall that incident, Mr. Marti?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please explain briefly, because it's already contained in your statement, what you saw at that time and which conclusions, if any, you made in relation to the shelling?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: When we were asked to go to this crater analysis in this village Vukovici, which is near to Cetina, we realised that the shellings were not as it was usually on a field, it -- the shellings were in a village. That means a house was hit by a grenade and the house, mainly the kitchen was destroyed. And I remember very well the four elderly women who were complaining about this incident and the detail I still remember that when the grenade came into the house, the watch on the wall stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti. I'll ask you a few more questions but if P211 could be brought up, which is a map of the Cetina area and I'd like you to mark, if you can, the location of Vukovici. While that's being done, can I ask you, looking back, do you remember whether you saw any military activity or military target in that village on that day?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: No. In that village, we didn't see any military target or military troops or whatever could have been a target to be shelled by a grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I think we have a better map. This is 65 ter 4938.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And while that's been done, Mr. Marti, who was doing the shelling on that day? Were you able to figure that out?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: No, we couldn't figure out who has done the shelling, we just could figure out where the shelling did come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where did it came from?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: It came from direction south-east, south south-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you point on this map which is now displayed on the screen where the village of Vukovici is?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: The village is here. And this is Cetina. And the shellings came from this direction so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you mark it?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. And the shells were fired from south-east?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes. Because it was an unusual -- if I may add something, it was an unusual crater analysis because that was a case where the shell was in a wall. So when you see the house, you can be very clearly where the shell has come from. It was even much more easier to deal with this crater analysis than when the crater was somewhere in an open field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you know the name of that mountain range where you say the shells were fired from?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: You mean the name of the mountains? That was the Dinara Mountains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, you marked the direction from where the shell came. Now, earlier, your testimony was that it was south south-east. What you marked on the map was -- seems to be east south-east.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we are talking in terms of the clock, it seems to be closer to 4.00 than to 5.00 which makes it not, for me at least, south south-east but east south-east. I'm just trying to clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was rather to -- if you take the picture of the clock it was rather from the direction to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which is east -- closer to east south-east, so closer to east than to south and from south-east. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know who occupied, at that time, in summer 1995, the Dinara mountains?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. Of course we heard some rumours but I have never seen somebody there so I cannot tell who actually was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if that could be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P418, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P418 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to go back to your 2007 statement which is P417 at paragraph 110. This is page 17 in the English version and page 19 in B/C/S. Let me briefly quote from your statement. "Concerning the issue of military operations, the military part, one has to say that prior to Operation Storm that the sporadic shelling around the area of Cetina to prevent farmers from harvesting had nothing to do with military activity, there were no military targets. The only purpose of the shelling was to intimidate the people and to prompt them to leave the area which they did." Now, Mr. Marti, what was the basis for your knowledge about what happened around these harvests, what you call "prevent farmers from harvesting"?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: If I can explain like this: I mean I also have some military experience because I was commander of a mortar company so I know a little bit basics of how to proceed with artillery shooting. But this artillery shooting was not according to any so-called traditional standards. I mean when you just have one shell somewhere and then for a while nothing happens then another grenade impacts somewhere, nothing happen anymore. Maybe it's finished for the whole day.
