And then maybe the next day, mainly in the evening, the shelling started again but very impromptu, you cannot say where it is. It was not -- we didn't see any -- we couldn't imagine that there was any real military target to be hit by an artillery grenade so for us, it was the -- and as we saw what actually happened was that the people get afraid and you know when you have children and you cannot -- no more be sure if the children are still safe and your family are safe, you start to first to remove the children, the family, and finally you leave yourself, the place. Also with discussion with the commander in Vrlika, he also told us, the UN must finish this shelling, otherwise we, the Serbian army, we also continue to shell Dubrovnik, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you when you say, "The UN must finish this shelling," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: I mean I had two or three meetings with Commander Popovic in Vrlika and the main problem was for him, I mean for the population, that the farmers were no more able to cut the corn, to do the harvest because they were afraid to go with a big cutting machine on the field during the day because they could never know if there would a grenade come. And I mean a machine to do the harvest is, in my opinion, not a military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This Commander Popovic you met, from which army was he?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Krajina Serb army in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last question on this issue: Did the UN conduct patrols in order to protect the farmers?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, we established a so-called harvest protection patrol. We divided this job with CIVPOL, that means half of the day UNMO patrol went into the Cetina area, just drive middle in the field, let the car standing in the field, put the flag on, and we were just hoping that if there is any artillery observer on the other side, he would see our UN car and hopefully he would not let any guns fired on us. And then the other half of the day, CIVPOL did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me turn back to the forces who did the shelling, the farmers, and Mr. Popovic complained about. Are you able to say who was the originator of this shelling that troubled the farmers?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: I mean when we did that crater analysis, what you can say very accurately was where, from which direction came the shelling, what calibre it was, but we never could state it really who had done it because we didn't have access to the other side. We could not go and -- to have a look there which Howitzer or whatever was on the other side. That was always -- also in our reports, we just noted the shelling comes from this and this direction. It had happened by this and this time, it had hit this and this field or whatever. But we were not able to make a statement who did it. I mean, because we didn't have access on the other side to find out where the places of the guns and howitzer on the other side were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti. If 65 ter 5189 could be retrieved. Now, in your 2007 statement, P417 now, at paragraph 28. This is page 5 in both English and B/C/S, you describe another incident of shelling that you experienced on the 30th of July. There has, in fact, Your Honours, been evidence led on this event in this courtroom already. Paragraph 28 mentions that you were on the way to conduct a crater analysis near Strmica when you came under fire from five to six shells. Mr. Marti, do you recall this incident when you came under fire?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I recall it very well because this was, I think, that the incident or the -- where I was most afraid in my whole year as a UN Military Observer because we were also called and it was like the other incidents and it was a Sunday too, we were called to make early Sunday morning crater analysis near Strmica. First we picked up the Serbian liaison officer in Knin and we drive towards Strmica and then we -- near Strmica, we parked the car and the liaison officer tried to get in contact with the Serb commander or whatever was there because there up in Strmica was also a checkpoint. When the man was away from us, all of a sudden the shelling started again and very close to us. I mean it was so close that I feel the impacts, the -- it was the air was shaking in my stomach, my whole body was shaking so we turned the car quick to go to a shelter near a stable. And I remember very well when I was turning the car, the interpreter told me we have to wait for the Serbian liaison officer because he was running towards us and we drive a small distance to the stable and beside the stable, we tried to have some protection, some shelter. By that time, there were about five to six impacts on the field nearby and it was -- by that time, I remember very well I was really afraid because I didn't know if the shelling comes closer, if it will finish or if there is -- if there was an artillery observer somewhere, if he would have seen us or if it was just an impromptu shelling near Strmica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti. Now, on your screen, you see a cut-out of an aerial of that Strmica area which we discussed during proofing. Now, can you indicate, using a pen Mr. Usher is providing you with, where you stopped the car and the liaison officer left it in order to make, as you say, contact with that Serbian checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: It must have been somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you mark it with A, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And second, the location where you thought at that time that the Serbian checkpoint was located.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: I think that the contact was somewhere here. But as I remember the checkpoint must be more up. I mean he didn't make a contact directly on the checkpoint. The checkpoint was -- I cannot actually remember very well if it was somewhere here. I remember there were two streets coming together but I cannot say from this map that these are exactly these two streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. So the circle to the top, the smallest one will be C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Make it a question mark in view of the witness' answer, he doesn't know whether it was there. If you put a question mark next to the small circle then ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And that delineates where you think might have been the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Checkpoint, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And lastly, if you can, mark the location of where you thought at the time that the shells were landing?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you could mark it with letter D, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: B or C?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: D, Daniel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could receive a number, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P419, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that P419 meets no objections? Then P419 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If D224 could be brought up, please. That's an excerpt, in fact, of Mr. Marti's diary that has been produced by the Defence with another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: While that's being done, let me ask you this, Mr. Marti: In the Cetina valley, did you see any signs of any weapons system that belonged to the Krajina Serb army?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: No, I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti. I'm only interested in the note at the bottom, Sunday, 30th July, 1995. And I read the portion in the middle line 5, "We picked up the LO at the North Dalmatian Corps, but then there was artillery shelling from Strmica on the western hillside about 1 kilometre away." Now, is that a correct English translation of your diary?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: No, this translation is not correct. When I read in my diary and if I may open the diary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may open the diary and I take it it's written in German. You would like to read in your own language, then, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to be very exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that will remain untranslated because we have no German-English translation. Nevertheless, it appears to be important to have it on the record. I do not know would to what extent the transcribing causes problems if the witness would speak German. If it cannot be transcribed, then at least it is on the audio record of this hearing and I think now sufficiently explained when there is a small gap. Please read slowly just the lines where you think that there is a translation error.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just read this sentence: "Beim Nord Dalmatien Korps LO aufgeladen, dann aber kurz vor Strmica Arty-shelling am Westhang, circa 1 Kilometer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you read it again so that I have it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Beim Nord Dalmatien Korps LO aufgeladen, dann aber kurz vor Strmica Arty-shelling am Westhang, circa 1 Kilometer. That means it was not near Strmica, but in -- before we reached Strmica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. So from Strmica is not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not correct. It's before we reached Strmica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you read in German "before"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Vor. Yes. Does this need any further clarification from my knowledge of the German language, "vor" means before you arrive somewhere or not "from." Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes this part of examination in chief about those events that occurred prior to Operation Storm. If we could bring up 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, before we -- of course it's nice if a witness reading the original and knowing how it's translated corrects what appears to be a translation error but would it not be the best way to replace the translation by a better one in e-court so that we -- if you would have done that, then -- and just have given notice of a correction then we do not have to bother the witness with it and we do not have to spend court time on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly we'll do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, I'm going to show you a series of six maps. In fact, I will only show you the first of these six maps and while that's being done, because it takes some time to upload it, can I ask you: Were you visited by investigators from the OTP who asked you to mark maps? The 65 ter number again is 4442.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: I was visited during my stay in Zagreb. By that time, I was still a UN Military Observer and I was posted by that time in Zagreb. That means not actually posted but we were waiting what would happen with the UN mission in Eastern Slavonia, so during that time I was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti. Mr. Registrar, if you could zoom in at the bottom of this map. Yes. Now, Mr. Marti, do you see some initials at the bottom of this map?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we move up, please, we can see yellow markings over village names. Can you tell the Court, Mr. Marti, who made these markings and what do they mean?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: It was me who has made this marking during this interview with the people from the court and as far as I remember, I marked all the places where UN patrols have been gone through, have noticed something or have found some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what time frame are we talking about that these UN patrols were operating?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: That time frame was after operation until November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And we know from your statement that you were a member and later a team leader of Team Podkonje. Did your team and you yourself participate in these patrols yourself?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are five more maps from other areas covering Sector South which have been marked by the witness. I don't think there is a need to go through them. With your leave, I would like to tender them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I hear from the Defence teams whether there's -- it appears that it's mainly identifying the maps and the markings, whether you are satisfied with this first map and take it as for a fact that the other maps are marked by this witness as well or would you like to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean I have no objection to a map such as this if it's just marking this as opposed to some -- if there's going to be some type of development from these other maps, then I think that they warrant a discussion that the Chamber may want to hear. If it's merely just a perfunctory marking of a document such as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The marking stands for something that is this is the villages where they went and where they have observed something during this period of time. I mean that's where we stand now, not any further details. Of course if we would go into further details, then of course we could check on this map whether that village was marked for having been visited and something we notice there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I suppose then if, in that sense, Judge, that the relevance of the other five maps escapes me if we are ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it says something, that's at least how I understand you, Mr. Waespi, that the area was visited with -- how do you say -- that the coverage of places visited was rather high and observations must have been rather frequent if you have so many markings on the map. Is that what you are seeking to establish?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. There is also a slight difference, as the witness will address later, between what the UNMOs did and what other international organisations did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So, therefore, also to identify UNMO as -- the UNMOs as the ones who visited these villages and these -- that's what it's for. If there's any objection -- Mr. Cayley not. Mr. Mikulicic, I do not see you have any objections. Mr. Kehoe the same. Then could you give the 65 ter numbers, all five, the first one, of course, we've got already. The next four ones so that Mr. Registrar can assign numbers to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the whole series of maps are unloaded under one number so therefore if Mr. Registrar now assigns a number, he assigns it to a series of maps marked out of court by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter 04442 becomes Exhibit number P420.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P420 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could see 65 ter 5187 which is a list of dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: While that's being done, Mr. Marti, do you recall the list that you see now on your screen?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And please tell the Court what this list is?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: This list with the date of 29th of November shows the dead bodies UN organisation has found in and around Knin in the former Sector South and -- but this list was not done by me, myself, but by the UN political affairs and what is on this list, you can see it on the right side, the list is not completed. There is another row with a row of the witnesses but this row is cut off due to security reasons. So when I got this list from Judy Jacobs, she told me I cannot hand it out this list to you because there are too -- the remarks of the witnesses are too sensitive. We have to be very careful that nobody -- that this list remains secret so I can only give you the list with the names, et cetera, where we have found the people, whom we have found, but not the list with the last row, so the last row of this list is cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, this new proposed exhibit is a part of already existing Exhibit P177 but it's a more legible copy at the right side. So with your leave, we would then, again, ask to replace that part of P177 which is pages P14 to P24. It is an identical copy although this copy obviously is a copy this witness received and not Mr. Anttila who was the tendering witness of P177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do I understand that it is 10 pages of P177 which contains this same list so therefore, we would not replace P177, but we would replace only a portion of that. Now, to what technical problems that will lead -- first of all, any objection against replacing part of P177 by a better, legible copy or by admission of this list?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The objection -- I don't normally object to these. The objection to this is that it is in fact different, I do believe, Judge. But more importantly, it's impossible for the Defence to get behind this document with the matters that have been taken off. I mean knowing the -- where this came from and where this information was compiled by that portion that has been taken off lends a tremendous amount of relevance to this document and certainly to the Defence. Now, the document that I think Mr. Waespi is talking about came in with Mr. Ermolaev, I believe, as -- Mr. Anttila, I believe, but this is a completely different document and before any admission of this document comes in, the Defence should be entitled to see the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What we see here, I think it's 11 pages, is according to my assessment, identical to those 11 pages that form part of P177. The only difference -- there are two difference. One difference is it's better legible and the second difference are the circumstances under which Mr. Marti received this copy. And the Defence is certainly allowed to explore more into the circumstances what might be missing. Mr. Marti already explained about the circumstances. And that's as far as I can take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if one looks at P177, the document that came in, this document is dramatically different from that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I tend to agree with you because it's a three- or four-column document only. The structure seems to be quite different. Now, apart from whether the Chamber would follow you in not admitting it, the document is quite different, Mr. Waespi, would you agree? If I look at -- if I look at the 10th page out of 24 on P177, first of all, it's a bit difficult to understand because the 9th page looks similar so I do not know exactly why it's only pages 10 to 14. The structure of the lists is quite different, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If that's the case, what the witness now discusses, which is ter 5187, that's a list the witness received at the date he hasn't told us yet from Ms. Jacobs from human affairs of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's keep matters simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's forget about replacing the list. Let's talk then about admission because that apparently is the remaining issue then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, one additional item which brings to mind the actual document that came in through Mr. Anttila. And when this document came in and it was handed over to the Defence, no one ever told us that the document was cut off and that there was yet another portion to this document that hadn't been provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, apart from that, Mr. Kehoe, of course that's a document dated the 4th of October, isn't it, and I don't know whether it was part of another document, parts cut off or whether it was another way of presenting the same data. I'm -- but let's not at this moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- let's not revisit the document which is in evidence but let's focus on admissibility of the present document where apparently two columns have been taken off. Could we first ask you, Mr. Marti, when you received this list which is now on your screen, were the two columns cut off already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I received this document in November in Knin when I was in the -- sorry, in Zagreb when I was in the UN HQ and I got this document from Judy Jacobs who was working with the UN in political affairs or whatever, I don't remember exactly. And she handed over this list to me and told me there are sensitive information on the original of this list. I cannot give you this -- the whole document due to reason of security. By that time, she also mentioned that her computer was stolen in inside the UN headquarters in Zagreb but as she did it every day or every evening, she always took the actual document, because this was an ongoing document, every evening, she took a copy on a disk --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at the time it was still disks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- home in her handbag, so it was okay. She got a new computer and continued her work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi. Yes. I don't know -- you objected against admission. I'd like to give an opportunity to Mr. Waespi to respond to that after we have gained some additional information from the witness. Mr. Kehoe, do you want to further elaborate on your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The first objection, obviously the document is not complete. The second objection is Mr. Marti can't even vouch for the accuracy of this document because it comes from Ms. Jacobs in political affairs. And it's very, very -- going at it further with regard to the sensitive information, it has to have -- bear some relevance on the content or it wouldn't have been deleted out. That merits some discussion. If the OTP has the whole document, I don't know if they do, Your Honour, it bears scrutiny at this point to look at the whole document and see where we can go from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, have you checked whether you have the whole document, that means including the cut-off -- I don't know whether they were electronically cut off or whether they were factually cut off. I see the witness making a gesture which appears to be scissors rather than electronically cutting it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, we were presented with this document, the physically cut-off document I think on Saturday for the first time by this witness. We saw the similarity to P177 and we thought it was important and indeed relevant that the witness told you about when he received the list, from whom he received the list, and whether there is additional information we might have witnesses from the UN, I think Mr. Al-Alfi is on our witness list who can shed further light on to this document. We don't have the cut-off part and the witness, Mr. President, Your Honours, I think is good enough to testify that he received this list from whom he received. He explained what was done with it and with all due respect, I think we have instances where documents were tendered with much, much less link to the tendering witness than in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The document that the witness got was a document with sensitive information which I understand or the sensitive information has been deleted. Now, whoever put this document together and it was not Mr. Marti, must have concluded that the information that was cut off bore some relevance to the items that are set forth in this document. Now, when this or some version of this was presented by Mr. Anttila, and I don't fault the Office of the Prosecutor in any fashion about this, and I don't think that they were informed of this, but apparently, the document or the version of this document that was presented by Mr. Anttila likewise had information that was cut off. At this point, Your Honour, this document, given it has just been told to the Defence that there was other information in here, puts us in a difficult position to scrutinise this document and the source of these allegations without the rest of this sensitive information because the document that is Prosecutor is offering is simply not a complete document and analogizing it to any other document one cannot just cut off that portion of the document simply to put it into evidence when one doesn't know what is actually being excised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To say cut off a part of the document to put it into evidence ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't infer anything negative from that and my apologies, I don't infer that and I have and I trust Mr. Waespi's word that he received this document in this fashion and I apologise if anything came along in that fashion. It wasn't meant that. What -- I'm just talking about is scrutinising this document as a whole and whether or not this document is -- certainly not a complete document, whether or not the Defence is, before such a document comes into evidence, should be permitted to scrutinise the whole because quite clearly, whatever has been excised off by Ms. Jacobs or whomever bore some significant relevance to the rest of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we first ask another a question to the witness. Mr. Marti, you explained to us that the list is not complete. There is, as you first said, another row. I later got the impression that there are actually two columns missing but I don't know whether you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how many columns exactly were still on the paper, but if you can see from the size of the version which is cut off and you took the whole page of -- the whole size of a page then you can see it must be one or maybe also two rows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Or it has been a two-page wide document which of course -- so but that's all conclusions. You say something is missing on the right. Now, you also told us that, "She told me that she could not hand it out to you because there are two remarks of the witnesses are too sensitive ..." Now, how did you -- I don't know if you have a recollection on how exactly she explained this to you. What kind of sensitivity she explained was contained in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She told me on the last row there are some remarks or names or something of who has witness -- who has been witness of these killed people, I mean who have seen what was going on when this 180-something dead bodies have been killed or who have found it first, et cetera. Because on the one row, you only see source of information, that is anonymous. For example, on number 4 it's just written "villagers" have found the people but not the name of the villagers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the sensitive nature of the information, did you understand it, that's at least how I now understand your words, was to -- not reveal the identity of the persons who had reported this or was there any other type of sensitivity involved in the cut-off parts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was only not to involve the -- persons in it who has made a statement towards the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, the -- with regard to identity, I mean if we just look at the source of information on the item that Mr. Marti said, the villagers, it says names are on file. So that would indicate that there is yet another file with the names of those individuals as opposed to the names of those individuals set forth in this document. But even if that were the case and it's just the names of the villagers, I think, Your Honour, based on some of the evidence that we have seen, that bears some scrutiny too. Because when these allegations which are very serious are set forth, who was making these allegations is equally serious because we have had in this court at least one witness who gave statements to the Office of the Prosecutor saying that he observed certain bodies at certain locations at the pertinent times, the first week in August of 1995 and then came into this courtroom and said that he did not see those bodies. So taking Mr. Marti from what he was saying, if that's, in fact, the case, that is equally important in order to flesh out some of these allegations that are in these documents -- in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can certainly make inquiries into whether the list exists in the UN system. We will contact Ms. Jacobs and can report back. But for the time being, I maintain my proposition to have this exhibit tendered as a document that Mr. Marti received directly from Ms. Jacobs and he explained the circumstances. It depends on the weight given to this document, if there are columns missing but it should certainly in our submission be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I do believe, Judge, and on the totality of matters, that this is a document that Mr. Marti didn't prepare, has no knowledge on the accuracy of this document because he didn't prepare it, it was simply given to him and it wasn't given to him in a complete form. And while he may have some inkling as to what is missing or not, the fact is that he doesn't know how much is missing. And I understand the weight to be given to a document but under the circumstances of offering a document that's not a complete document through a witness that didn't prepare it and doesn't know anything about the accuracy of it, I think we are beyond the admissibility point and I don't think there is any foundation for this document to come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will take the break to decide on admissibility. I don't know, Mr. Waespi, whether you would have any further questions in relation to this document because then of course we might consider to take an early break but if you have no questions on the document, it will now be marked for identification. The Chamber will decide on admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P421 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could move to probably a less controversial document, 65 ter number 2023. This is a document dated 10th of September, 1995. If we can briefly go to the last page of this short document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We see here, Mr. Marti, that your name appears and if we can go to the front page again. Mr. Marti, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you please explain to the Court what it is?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: It was a report done on the 10th of September, 1995, when I was -- just a few days after I have been appointed as team leader of Team Podkonje and we register some people we have found who are still -- who were still living in the area and I also described that the problems we had, we faced because it was almost impossible as a team leader with -- in the best case, three teams cover all the area and try to find out who is still living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like you to refer to one specific part of the document and it's in both English and B/C/S on the first page. The heading "Two problems: One, humanitarian aid is not usual task for UNMOs ..." and so on. And the last sentence in this paragraph in English on page 2 says, and I quote, "What are the other international organisations really doing on the ground more than driving along the main asphalt roads?" Can you explain what you meant when you wrote that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: During that time, there were different organisations busy in Knin like UNHCR, like the European Commission Mission also some other -- even some NGOs also Red Cross. But we realised that along the main roads, the remaining people were visited sometimes several times by the different organisations but in the small hamlets up in the mountains, nobody was there, even we didn't know exactly who was still living there. And the UNMOs were the only one who were able to proceed in these villages and hamlets because of the fact that we had four-wheel driven cars and we had also all the accurate maps and the knowledge about the region so UNMOs were the only one who were able to travel in all the small places but the task was almost impossible to fulfill because we were only a few. I mean I had about 8, 9 people in my team and when somebody was on the normal leave, I was able to let conduct two patrols, in the best case, three. So the task to get an overview of what was going on in the region was almost impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And concluding this document, can you briefly tell the Court the -- whether the people you visited, the villagers appreciated your presence?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, they appreciated it very much because in many cases, we were the only one who were in contact with them. I remember a case in Mrkic, that is near Otric, we found up in the mountains, we found an old couple and they didn't realise that there has been a war down in the valley. So they just tell us that they had no electricity anymore, but that was all. So we were the first ones who gave them the information that there has been a war. Or in another case, I remember very well in a small hamlet in Plavno valley a woman told me, "You are like the sun," when we were coming. And it was very emotional situations because they hug us and they even kissed us and they were -- you can see that what was missing was not in the first case food or -- but contact and information what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti. And I think you referenced to the sun and "sunce" in Croatian is mentioned on page 2 of the English document under 3, comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this document could be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. I see no objections from any of the Defence teams. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P422, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P422 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could move to the next document and already existing Exhibit P68 at page 17, second paragraph from the bottom in English and it's on page 14, B/C/S, third paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This reference, Mr. Marti, is to a visit of your team to several villages including Biskupija on the 26th of August, 1995. Do you remember this patrol, Mr. Marti?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember very well because that very day was my birthday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we look what's written down on that paragraph, it says that and I quote, from the third line, "... and observed that most of the houses were looted, many were burned down. The few villagers are scared of the presence of HV soldiers." Now, can you describe to the Court the appearance of these HV soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: They were partly dressed with --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, are we talking about this particular instance or are we talking about generally? Because I don't think that the witness says that the HV soldiers were there on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, we'll talk about these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take care that you clarify whether you're talking general or whether on these specific incidents. Mr. Marti, you might have catched up already some of the problems when you are -- describe the appearance of HV soldiers, whether you are describing any HV soldiers you may have seen at that occasion, if there were any, or whether you are describing HV soldiers in more general terms. I mean not specifically for this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, what I'm interested in is whether you recall the presence of these HV soldiers on your birthday in 1995 in any of those villages?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: I think on the way back when we were on patrol in the evening near Ocestovo, we were stopped by four -- I will call it soldier because they have military guns and they have still part of military uniform. So for me, this were type of soldiers. And we were first -- I remember because my Kenyan colleague was the driver. I was the patrol leader. And it was near Ocestovo in a small forest. We were stopped by these four young men and first I thought: Should we try to just to drive through because we had an armoured car. But then I decide, okay, I am not a driver and I cannot tell the Kenyan colleague to speed up so we better stop. But when you have an armoured car, you cannot open the windows so to talk with people, with these guys, I had to open my door and I was quite nervous because I didn't know what would happen so I just used my few words which I knew by that time in Croatian and tried to explain the man who I am, what I am doing so I showed him the map and told him with my fingers, I want to go from here to here and then they just let us pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could get 65 ter 5192, please. And, Your Honours, this is a newspaper excerpt we received from the witness on Saturday and which we disclosed to the Defence. It's four pages, I believe, and I'm interested in two photos the witness explained to us during the proofing session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you first, Witness Marti, when did you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: On the 10th of August, just shortly after the Operation Oluja, our sector commander Lieutenant-Colonel Steinar Hjertnes gave us a day free. That means he told us, my team had the chance to go to the UN team in Sibenik to have at least a fresh shower after so many days and just to relax and come back the next day. And due to my former profession, I was very much interested in newspapers so that very day in Sibenik, I -- even if I couldn't understand the words but I tried to buy as much as newspaper from that very day and among these newspapers were both these pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And does the photo or the soldiers, one of the soldiers depicted on this photo remind you of soldiers you have seen during the patrol activities?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, it does, especially the soldier here in front because for my understanding by that time of how an army should be at least look like, that was something which was not used so I called them in my private diary pirate soldiers. For me they look rather than pirates than members of a military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where did you see these pirate soldiers, as you call them in your diary?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: They looked very similar to what I have mentioned before near Ocestovo on the 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page or I guess the third page or do we only have this photo uploaded? The next page, please. Yes. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Is there another photo here that reminds you of pirate soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, this photo on the top which -- a man who is handing -- making -- who is receiving fire from the soldier with the helmet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, if this exhibit could be tendered into evidence? I'm, in fact, only interested in the two photos the witness described and not in any text there might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would like to say something. Does the admitting of these photographs includes and likewise the text below them because I think the text below them is very significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So I have no objections as to introduce as evidence those photographs but I would like that also the text would be admitted as in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Obviously the witness doesn't read or at least not sufficiently to understand what he bought on, I think, the 10th of August, but I have absolutely no problem to have the whole thing admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know what the text is under there, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen the line, it says Kijevo, it says Knin and it has a few lines of explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm especially referring to the first photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. The text below it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The text below it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The text below it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it appears that Mr. Waespi has no objection so therefore -- but you have not uploaded any translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, that's the main reason why I only tendered the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, and that of course also makes the importance of this evidence very relative is that is what we see on this picture resembles more or less the type of military people that you've seen at that date. So it's a rather, I would say, a rather impressionist piece of evidence. Now, if we add text to that, I have got no idea what the text is, whether it is favourable or unfavourable to either of the parties. Then of course we get a photograph of which we do not know when it was taken, where it was taken, we also all are aware that the media have not always for the full 100 per cent been neutral on reporting on war situations. If you would keep all of this in mind that you would still be happy to have the text admitted then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no reason not to admit the photos, at least the two photographs with text but with a clear signal that what weight to be given to this text, it could be about being a guitar on the one and an accordion on the other picture, we've got no idea but let's look at it, take care that it will be uploaded with translation. May I take it that we leave it to just the text related to these two photographs because otherwise we really are too far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P423.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P423 is admitted into evidence. The Prosecution is instructed to provide translation of the photograph on the front page and the photograph on the third page including an accordion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to go to another document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you moving to another subject as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we rather first have the break. Apart from having a break, Mr. Waespi, I think the witness was scheduled for two and a half hours. I think you've until now -- we had a bit of a procedural incident but approximately five-quarters of an hour. Are you confident that you will manage before we adjourn for the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think another hour I anticipate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we quickly go for the break. Resume at quarter to 1.00. Precisely, you've got one hour left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document marked for identification P421, that is the list is admitted into evidence. At the same time, Mr. Waespi, you offered that the Prosecution would further inquire into the -- to whether there was a complete version of this list already available and also to further investigate whether the source that provided the witness -- provided the list to this witness, whether that person could provide us with a complete list. You are invited to report on that within -- how much time do you think it would take you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think that's going to be communication with New York so two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two weeks. You are instructed to report within two weeks what the results of your further inquiries are. Of course the Chamber has considered the objections against admission and the Chamber will in giving weight to the document, the Chamber will certainly have in the back of its mind the objections made. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If Prosecution Exhibit P176 could be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, I understand from your witness statement that your Team Podkonje was involved in assessing the damage caused by Operation Storm and in the aftermath to the houses in the area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me show you a document and if we can go to page 2. You are also familiar, I take it, with Mr. Anttila.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what does this document show?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: It gives an overview about the damages in the different villages of the region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to page 7 of this document in both versions, and I think it's just -- if it could be enlarged a bit, the English part. We see, Mr. Marti, that the bottom half of the document lists Team Podkonje with some activity and as you see from the document, there are other columns with data that's filled in. And in relation to the heading "number of buildings," we see that there is a lack of data for Team Podkonje. Now, do you have an explanation why Team Podkonje didn't report as completely as perhaps other teams on number of buildings in certain villages and towns?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I have an explanation because our main focus was not on the destroyed or partly destroyed buildings. Our main focus was on the people who were still living in the area. So we rather tried to find people who were still there than to count all the houses or partly damaged houses. I mean we just tried to establish a kind of system to get an overview about the whole situation in the region of Krajina and some teams put their attendance more on the buildings, how were the buildings and my teams, we were always -- our main focus was on the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's turn to the last page of this document which shows the summing up of these figures and if it can be made slightly more bigger still, you can see that between the number of buildings reported, above 20.000, and the number of buildings damaged or partially damaged, there is perhaps a ratio of two-thirds of the buildings at least partially damaged. Now, you have been there in that region, you were on numerous patrols, you were patrol leader. Can you tell the Court whether that ratio, as we see it here in Mr. Anttila's study, is an accurate one? Does it coincide with your own assessment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object, Judge, there's no foundation for that. The foundation has got to come from the actual numbers and you just can't add -- you add numbers to the numerator and not to the denominator and it skews the percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm less interested in the exact percentage. I would just like the witness to tell the Court whether according to his personal knowledge, his capacity as a member, as a team leader, roughly that picture displayed in this survey coincides with what he has observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I quite simply object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just ask the witness whether he could give us a general impression of the percentage of buildings that was partially or totally damaged, then you don't give him the clue of the answer which, of course, is leading in some way. Could you give us your impression about the percentage of houses that do remain not undamaged so that were either partly or totally destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can at least try because it was -- there were some villages which were more or less completely destroyed but some other mainly small hamlets up in the mountains which have not been touched by the war. But overall average is about 60 per cent of the buildings were partly or completely destroyed and even we made a difference because in the region, of course, you also found buildings who have been destroyed or partly destroyed much earlier, that means before Operation Oluja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can move on to the next exhibit, potential exhibit, this is ter number 620. For everybody's understanding, this is a note for the record dated 15 -- in fact, 16 September, 1995, although the actual report that starts on page 2 is a note dated 15 September 1995. If we can go to page two in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Marti, do you recognise this document and what it's about?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this document and it covers the case where we -- UN organised a transport for the people who have been left in the area but who wanted to be transported towards Serbia to their relatives or whatever. Because whenever we found people before, we also asked them, What are your problems, do you want to stay here or do you want to leave and whenever they tried -- they wanted to leave, there was something like a collection point organised in the school of Knin and the UN helped the people to go there and at that very day, there was a -- in my opinion, a very fast way was a transport organised from Knin to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I see on line 3 of the first paragraph, Plavno. A sentence and I quote, "They had been threatened by the army and their houses looted; some had been damaged." Do you remember this instance of threats by the army and looted houses?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: What I remember is that the people we found there had complained that they are no more sure that nobody helps them, nobody protects them. They are afraid. They just want to be -- to live in safe conditions again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti. If that could be admitted as an exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P424, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P424 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Waespi, when you used this inventory of buildings, et cetera, did you check whether, because it looks very much like a - how do you call it - a spreadsheet where you usually say at the bottom, some this, some that. Now we often see that either the total number of buildings is not filled in but sometimes the damage to buildings is there in numbers. Sometimes it's the other way around that we have the total number of buildings but not even not zeros for partially damaged or totally destructed. Now, if I, at the bottom end, say some column so and so, then you get the distortion, have you verified, has someone verified how these numbers at the very end, what they actually do sum up? Because then you get different data.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll certainly look into that. I think at least four witnesses have been testified as to this document. I think there are even four different versions of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: With Mr. Ermolaev, Mr. Anttila, Mr. Munkelien and now with this witness and I agree that there might be enough information now to assess the reliability and the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not that impressed that comments are there by other witnesses on the matter where the witnesses might not have been fully aware of the way in which the spreadsheet was handled. But I'm just drawing your attention to it because you are now specifically focused on the last line which summarizes, but I would like to know what exactly it summarizes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just briefly with regard to this document and the content of P176, the only witness that said anything about the content of that document was Mr. Anttila. To the extent that Mr. Ermolaev said he was received the document but he was the only one that had any degree of discussion about it because he was one of the preparers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was only drawing the attention that if you look at the sums, you should know exactly what is summed. Otherwise, it might distort the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, that goes to -- because the sums include damage prior to Storm and, of course, it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's another aspect. But I'm -- I am aware of that. Nevertheless, it even goes further than that alone. Yes, because that is more or less specifically identified not in their numbers but at least in the comments whereas this might just slip in without anyone noticing. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If potential exhibit 65 ter number 2038 could be pulled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Marti, in your witness statement of 2007 which is now P417, at paragraph 12, you discuss that you have met once a person called Milan Marcetic and you said that you were informed that he had been killed at a later stage. Can you please look at this document and more importantly at the second page of this document which is an incident report by CIVPOL dated the 12th October, 1995. Now, do you see a reference to the death of Milan Marcetic?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see. I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in your diary, do you have a reference, if you recall, to the fact that Mr. Marcetic was reported killed? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I have a reference in my diary because I got to know some days later that he has been killed and I mean he was somebody who I have seen alive and I -- even when I met him, I was wondering because he is a man who was still there and normally, the Serb men, they had to run away or they run away. But he was still alive and I ask him, Why you are here? Why you are alive? Why you were never harmed by anybody or so? And then he told me he has never been in the Yugoslavian army because he is -- his eyes are not good enough and you could see it from his glasses, they were really thick glasses so he was unable to do military service. And even he showed me a paper but of course I couldn't read it because it was all in Cyrillic letters but he told me that this is paper that proves that he has never been in the army. He showed that paper to the soldiers when they arrived and that was the reason why they left him in peace. Then when some days after, when I got to know that he was killed, then I was very disappointed because I saw all -- what we are trying to protect the people there actually it was not a guarantee that the people were protected. I mean in our opinion, it was -- the minimum we could do, we said, okay, at least we make a list of all the people who are still there so that might be a kind of protection and everybody knows we have registered the people. They cannot just disappear after. But still that was not any type of protection as the case of Milan Marcetic showed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Mr. Marti, in paragraph 12 of your witness statement, P417, you mention the death of another person. Do you remember who that second person was?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: I have to go to my diary to find out the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, with Mr. President's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please try to find the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The 8th of October although there might be a --

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, in my diary I wrote in my diary that I get to know Milan Marcetic and Dusan Suica have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Marti. Now, on the screen in front of you, you have already recognised the name of Mr. Marcetic. Do you see also the name of the second person?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yeah, I think -- yes, it must be on the second-last paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti. Mr. President, if that document could be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. First objection, of course, is this is outside of time frame that Your Honour limited for the indictment. I do believe Your Honour gave an order on that score limiting the time frame to be addressed by the Prosecution's case. The second issue on this is that this is not within an area of responsibility with regard to my client. It's not within the Split Military District. Because I do believe from the top front page of this document, we're talking about the village that's in the Gracac area. Frankly, I mean with regard to the probative value of it, it's a statement that was taken by UN CIVPOL that, with all due respect to Mr. Marti, he doesn't know anything about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do the other Defence teams share the objections? Yes, I see yes from the Cermak team. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although your microphone was not switched on, I do understand that the Markac Defence has no objections, that the Cermak Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I share the objections with Mr. Kehoe. I have no objections of my own, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I misunderstood you. So all three Defence teams object against submission. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think the death occurred, according to paragraph 12 of P417 on the 29th, on or about the 29th of September, 1995, which is within the indictment period as I understand. In relation to the location, I have to verify that but it's certainly in the former Sector South area as defined by the UN, otherwise the witness wouldn't talk about. Thirdly, on its face, this document clearly appears to be authentic and the witness can be cross-examined about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Frankly, Judge, I can't cross-examine him about the document because, with all due respect, Mr. Marti doesn't know anything about this particular document. The fact is that this area is not within my client's area of responsibility and I think that that's just a fact that is well-known to the Prosecution as well. To set out yet with another homicide in an area that is not his responsibility is prejudicial and we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I haven't heard you about the time limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will go back and take a look at this. I know that the time limit, I was looking at the front page here which notes that this report is dated October 7th, 1995. Getting behind this document, certainly if it's something that's in and around that time frame, it's outside the -- it's outside the time frame of this investigation. If we look at the third page of this document, with the HRAT activities, that's in fact noted on the 9th of October. I would say that both of these note -- it does note the 29th of September but at this point, if -- certainly I can't ask Mr. Marti about the underlying facts on the score because he doesn't know anything about it. So if we could take an additional look at exactly when this information was transmitted, I think it may be outside the time-frame at which at first blush it looks like it might be of the matters covered by this indictment. So, if we could cover this just as an MFI at this point then do further research, I will consult with my colleague on the time-frame and see whether it goes into that appropriate time-frame as delineated by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please MFI the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P425, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi, you are invited to see to what extent an agreement can be reached with Mr. Kehoe. The Trial Chamber will take care that by the beginning of tomorrow morning's session that you -- that the Defence is aware whether it's admitted, yes or no. Please proceed. Of course at the beginning we'll tell you unless we receive other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's turn to the shelling of Knin. Mr. Marti, in all three of your witness statements you gave observations about the shelling of Knin on the 4th and 5th August and we'll come to that in a second. Now, where were you when Knin was shelled on the 4th and 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: On the 4th of August, 1995, I was in Podkonje the whole day. And on the 5th of August, I was in UN camp, UN headquarter in Knin itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me direct you to your witness statement of December 2007, that's P417 at paragraph 110. That's on page 17 in the English and page 19 in B/C/S. We -- I already quoted from this paragraph in relation to the Cetina shelling. Let me continue at around line 6. And I quote, "The same is to be said for the shelling of Knin which is clearly a violation of laws and customs of war. It is forbidden to shell a civilian town, of course one could assume that there might have been military personnel in the town, but there was no real military target. The only thing which might have been there was a camp close to the UN camp, a place where there were a few tanks and a repair depot were located but it was so close to the UN camp that its targeting would have been useless. The shelling, in fact, took place without a goal. It was carried out rather randomly. It was carried out above all to intimidate the people and to force them out which eventually happened. And they also fired at the refugees, one could see that later on the road, one could see craters, artillery craters on the road, and on the road there are no military targets only if there are tanks on the street, however tanks, destroyed tanks were hardly to be seen, one could see many civilian vehicles." And I might add that this is an excerpt from your taped statement which you gave in 1997, originally in German. Now, can you comment on what you said here? What was the basis for your assessment which I just read out?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: The basis of this quote I made in 1997 was my experience as far as I have been in Knin and around Knin, I never saw a big military target which could have been or should have been taken under fire by artillery. I mean when you take a target under fire by artillery, it must be a couple of tanks or a couple of vehicles or -- it must be a bigger target, not only one building or so. So when the attack on Knin started on the 4th of August, we were rather surprised because we didn't know what's going on and it was also not traditional artillery shelling, it was one shot then after a time another one and you could see -- I mean we couldn't see directly from Podkonje to Knin, but because there was a small hill in between but what we could see, we could see that smoke rose up from different places but even by that time there was -- the people were not yet in panic. I mean, we lived together with the people in this small village, Podkonje, we didn't know what is going on, just during the day the shelling of Knin continued but not with a clear aim. Later on when we were allowed to go and -- to leave the camp, the UN camp in Knin, we realised on the street, mainly on the street towards Otric that there have been artillery shelling on the street, into the street and we saw civilian vehicles hit, destroyed. We saw items from population left like clothes, furniture all along the street. That means they -- there have been civilian shelled by artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you discuss among the UNMOs the comment you just made?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed this case several times among UNMOs but after the operation was over, our main focus was as I have mentioned already, just to see what happens with the people which were not able to flee, which were not able to run away. Are they protected? Or what happened to them? And that was our main point to find out if after the operation, is there a security provide for the people or is there now, if one -- one government has been pushed out, if there is now a new control on the ground and we didn't see much or we didn't see that there was done much for the security of the people left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a moment, the control aspect of it. Let me show you 65 ter number 5188. Did you see houses burning, Mr. Marti, in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, on different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Looking at this photo, can you tell us what it depicts?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: It is a burning stable which I saw together with my Swedish colleague, Mr. Bertil Svendsen when we were on patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court when you took this photo?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, but I have again to stick to my diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please consult your diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the Court is also interested in the location of this burning house.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it. It was on the 4th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the location?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: It's called -- the name is called Ivosevci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Ivosevci.

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Ivosevci, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know where it is in relation to Kistanje?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: It's on the way to -- it's north, a few kilometres north of Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see houses, Mr. Marti, that were apparently safe from being burned because they were marked as Croatian houses?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: No, I didn't see such houses. I can only remember that in our neighbourhood in Knin when we got a new location, the neighbour woman, she -- one day she painted on her house "kuca Hrvatska" or similar like this, that means that this is a Croatian house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the effect of the marking of the house as a Croatian house, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: I think the main effect was to mark the house was also a kind of self-protection but I don't know if it works all the time. I mean I can see in our -- in -- what I can say in our neighbourhood, it works because this woman, she was not -- the house was not -- didn't get destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, why would she, if you know, mark her house as a Croatian house?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: I actually, the neighbouring woman, she was a Croatian woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the purpose of her doing that is what?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: Just to show the looters that they shouldn't loot or destroy this house also.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marti. Let me address in the remaining minutes the aspect of control or measures. In your taped witness statement which is now P416, if that could be pulled up, please. But before we do that, Mr. President, if we could have an exhibit number for this photo, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P426, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P426 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. P416, page 13, English version, and page 12 in B/C/S. In the English version it's line 28, towards the bottom. Let me quote. "The question whether the looting could have been prevented, I must actually answer with yes. It would indeed have been possible for the Croatian authorities which after all claimed that this area belonged to them, that is, was their territory and who made us sometimes feel that it would have been indeed possible for them to establish more order. It would not have been impossible to set up at the main crossings, at the main intersections police checkpoints and it would also have been necessary to make a deterrent example with adequate reports in the media to prevent these lootings," and it goes on to the next page, "and the threatening of the old people or at least largely reduce them but as already mentioned, nothing happened. Almost nothing happened." Now, can you elaborate a bit, Mr. Marti. Why do you say the Croatian authorities could have done more?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: As I have mentioned already, to do our job was something like almost an impossible thing. I mean we tried to protect somehow the remaining people but with our few patrols just noticed the name of the people that was actually not done with it. And we were always wondering why the Croatian authorities, whoever, police, or army or whoever, but I mean they have overtaken Krajina so now they also were responsible for the security there, why they didn't do more to provide security. For example, when you saw the looting in Plavno valley, this is a valley surrounded by mountains and there is only one or two streets leading into this valley, one checkpoint there would have reached to stop the looting in Plavno valley. One checkpoint maybe on the street crossing in Kistanje would have at least reduced the looting. One checkpoint in Vrlika, et cetera, only with a few means, you could have established something like a little bit of order. Of course when we -- we also tried to -- what we could do against the looters? I mean when we were on the spot with our UN vehicle, they just disappear or sometimes even we get into discussion with them. Once I ask a looter what he is doing here and he told me I'm just looking for a motor saw. So I mean looting was something like shopping without paying. Or in other cases, we start to discuss many times also in German because many of them have been in Germany and Switzerland before, and then they also told us, oh, where UN have been, 1991 when we have been pushed out from Krajina. I mean on one side, I understood that there was also revenge behind -- to come back in they told us, oh, that was my house several years ago so I'm just back now. But what I said with this statement was that if there was an authority, and there was an authority who pretend to be responsible for Krajina now, because they had a big - how you say - a big party on 26th of August when Tudjman came by train through Knin to Split, that was also on my birthday by the way, so I mean when you have overrun a region, then you are responsible. You are responsible for security. But I mean where has this brigade gone who has attacked Knin and Krajina before? As I remember on a map in a newspaper, there were about five brigades who have been attacked Krajina. So what they did afterwards? Why they didn't provide more security there? It would have been not so difficult just to establish different checkpoints. Then at least when the people realise that there is a control, they would have changed hopefully their behaviour. Just one detail. One of our -- we thought we could do something so we started to notice the number plate of the cars who came and looted the villages and we gave them to the Croatian authorities. But a few days after, what happened, the cars just came without number plates. So at least that shows that somebody has realised that somebody is making a very small kind of control so they realised that we were controlling something but that was not enough. And I remember we discussed this also with Croatian authorities and then for only a few days, there was a checkpoint near -- where the street comes out from Plavno valley and we thought, okay, at least now we have achieved something, a small stone for security. But a few days afterwards, this checkpoint was not manned again, it was empty. What can we do?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In your witness statement I quoted a moment ago, you talk about the necessity of a deterrent example with adequate reports in the media. Can you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: PETER MARTI
utterances.text: I'm quite sure if the Croatian officials would have stated officially that it is not allowed to loot and that the looters are punished and even maybe if they would have made an example public, okay, we have catch this and this person with looting things, now he has to give it back or whatever, that most probably would have helped a little bit but there was -- there was nothing against it and I mean it was funny, you could see the -- a kind of looting procedures. The first wave, what they took, the remaining cars, TV, washing machines, you could see it -- what they have put on their cars.
